entry: German social democratic politician and socialist theorist. Bernstein is best known for his reformist challenge to [[Marxism]], known as evolutionary socialism or revisionism. In *Evolutionary Socialism* (1899), he questioned the revolutionary predictions of [[Karl Marx]], rejected the Hegelian [[Dialectic|dialectical method]], and disputed Marx's forecasts of capitalism's inevitable collapse. He argued that socialists should pursue gradual reforms through democratic institutions, a focus captured in his aphorism "the goal is nothing, the movement everything." Born in [[Berlin]] to a lower-middle-class Jewish family, he spent years in exile in [[Switzerland]] and [[London]] during the Anti-Socialist Laws, where he became a close associate of [[Friedrich Engels]]. The [[Social Democratic Party of Germany|SPD]] officially condemned his views, though its practical policies were largely reformist. During [[World War I]] he co-founded the anti-war Independent Social Democratic Party, and he later served in the Reichstag during the [[Weimar Republic]].

Soviet and Georgian politician and diplomat. He was First Secretary of the Georgian Communist Party from 1972 to 1985, making him the de facto leader of [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]], and he launched economic reforms that spurred growth in the republic. In 1985 [[Mikhail Gorbachev]] appointed him Soviet minister of foreign affairs, a post he held until the fall of the [[Soviet Union]], apart from a brief interruption in 1990–91. After the Soviet collapse he led Georgia as Chairman of Parliament from 1992 and was elected president in 1995. His presidency included a 1993 victory in the Georgian Civil War, and the Sochi agreement ended military hostilities in [[South Ossetia]], though Georgia lost effective control over a large part of the territory. In 1999 Georgia acceded to the [[Council of Europe]], and in 2002 he declared Georgia's intention to join [[NATO]]. His rule was marked by corruption and accusations of nepotism. Allegations of electoral fraud in the 2003 legislative election led to the Rose Revolution protests, and he agreed to resign.

Norwegian painter and printmaker. His *The Scream* (1893) became one of the most iconic images in Western art, and its agonized face is widely identified with the angst of the modern person. Between 1893 and 1910 Munch made two painted versions and two pastels of the subject, as well as prints. After studying in Kristiania ([[Oslo]]), he was influenced by the bohemian circle there and by [[Paul Gauguin]], [[Vincent van Gogh]] and [[Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec]] in Paris. He worked on a series he called *The Frieze of Life*, depicting love, anxiety, jealousy and betrayal, and his work is regarded as pioneering [[Expressionism]]. Beginning in 1894 he engraved directly onto copper, producing a substantial body of prints. A mental breakdown in 1908 led him to give up heavy drinking. His works were banned in Nazi-occupied Europe, but most of them survived World War II.

Austrian-born American pioneer of [[Public relations|public relations]] and propaganda. Called "the father of public relations" in his obituary, Bernays wrote *Crystallizing Public Opinion* (1923) and *Propaganda* (1928), early efforts to define the field. His best-known campaigns included a 1929 effort to promote women's smoking by branding cigarettes as "Torches of Freedom," and work for the [[United Fruit Company]] in the 1950s, linked to the 1954 coup in Guatemala. He also worked for [[Procter & Gamble]] and [[General Electric]]. He described crowds as irrational and outlined how practitioners could use crowd psychology and the psychoanalysis of his uncle, [[Sigmund Freud]], to influence them. He is credited with advancing the profession, but critics argue that his techniques manipulated public opinion and undermined democratic values. *Life* named him one of the 100 most influential Americans of the twentieth century.

English composer. His best-known works include the *Enigma Variations* (1899), the *Pomp and Circumstance* marches, concertos for violin and cello, and two symphonies, as well as the choral work *The Dream of Gerontius* (1900). Raised a [[Catholic Church|Roman Catholic]] in Protestant Britain and largely self-taught, he struggled for success until his forties, when the *Enigma Variations* became immediately popular in Britain and overseas. In his fifties he composed a symphony and a violin concerto that were immensely successful. His later works came to be seen as appealing chiefly to British audiences, and his reputation revived in the 1960s. He made acoustic recordings from 1914 to 1925 and, after the introduction of the moving-coil [[Microphone|microphone]] in 1923, re-recorded most of his major orchestral works. He was appointed Master of the King's Musick in 1924.

British essayist, historian and politician. His most important work, *The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire*, was published in six volumes between 1776 and 1789, to critical and commercial success. It is known for the quality and irony of its prose, its use of primary sources, and its polemical criticism of organized religion. After converting to Roman Catholicism at Magdalen College, Oxford, in 1753, Gibbon was sent to live under the care of a Reformed pastor in [[Switzerland|Lausanne]], where he reconverted to Protestantism on Christmas Day, 1754. There he formed one of his two great friendships, with the French-language translator of Goethe's *The Sorrows of Young Werther*.

American [[Realism (arts)|realist]] painter and [[Printmaking|printmaker]]. Hopper's paintings, often set in New York City or the architectural landscapes of [[New England]], depict loneliness and isolation in American urban and rural life, using light and shadow to evoke mood. His best-known work, *Nighthawks* (1942), depicts a quiet, introspective scene from everyday life. He gained recognition in the 1920s, and his works were featured in major American museums. In 1924 he married the artist Josephine Nivison, who managed his career and modeled for many of his works. The couple spent summers on [[Cape Cod]], which influenced his later art. The [[Museum of Modern Art]] held a retrospective of his work in 1933, and he represented the United States at the 1952 Venice Biennale.

King of England (r. 1327–1377). Edward restored royal authority after the disastrous reign of his father, [[Edward II]], and transformed England into one of the most formidable military powers in Europe. At 17 he led a [[Coup d'état|coup]] against Roger Mortimer, the de facto ruler, and began his personal reign in 1330. After declaring himself rightful heir to the French throne, he started the [[Hundred Years' War]] (1337–1453). Victories at Crécy and Poitiers led to the Treaty of Brétigny (1360), under which England gained territory in France. His 50-year reign, one of the longest in English history, saw the evolution of the English Parliament, while the [[Black Death]] ravaged the population. Later failures and poor health brought setbacks, and by 1375 England had lost most of his conquests except Calais. Whig historians denounced him as an irresponsible adventurer, but modern historians credit him with significant achievements.

King of England (r. 1307–1327). His relationship with the favorite Piers Gaveston provoked discontent among the barons. He was defeated by [[Robert the Bruce]] at Bannockburn in 1314. In 1326 his wife, Isabella, and Roger Mortimer invaded England, and he was forced to relinquish the crown to his son, [[Edward III]]. He died at Berkeley Castle, probably murdered on the orders of the new regime. [[Christopher Marlowe]]'s 1592 play *Edward II* was inspired by Edward's relationship with Gaveston.

King of England (r. 1461–1470; 1471–1483). A member of the [[York|House of York]], he was a central figure in the [[Wars of the Roses]]. He deposed Henry VI in 1461 after victories at Mortimer's Cross and Towton. He returned from [[Flanders]] in 1471 to regain the throne after a brief restoration of Henry VI. He invaded France in 1475 but agreed to the Treaty of Picquigny with [[Louis XI]], which formally ended the [[Hundred Years' War]]. After his sudden death in 1483, his sons disappeared and his brother seized the throne as Richard III.

King of England (r. 1272–1307), also known as Edward Longshanks. Edward reformed royal administration and the common law through [[Statute|statutes]] regulating criminal and property law, and he established Parliament as a permanent institution. He conquered Wales in 1282–83 and built castles and towns there, settled with English people. He claimed feudal suzerainty over Scotland and invaded it, starting the First Scottish War of Independence, which continued after his death. He also fought France over Gascony, and his heavy taxation met opposition from both lay and ecclesiastical quarters. Historians praise his contributions to law and administration but criticize his uncompromising attitude toward the nobility. The 1290 Edict of Expulsion, which expelled all Jews from England, is among his most condemned policies. He was crowned at [[Westminster Abbey]] in 1274 and was succeeded by his son, [[Edward II]].

English physician and scientist who pioneered vaccination. In 1796 he created the smallpox vaccine, the world's first, and the terms [[Vaccine|vaccine]] and [[Vaccination|vaccination]] derive from *Variolae vaccinae* ("pustules of the cow"), his term for cowpox. His 1798 *Inquiry into the Variolae vaccinae known as the Cow Pox* described the protective effect of cowpox against [[Smallpox]]. Jenner is often called "the father of [[Immunology|immunology]]," and smallpox had killed about 10% of the global population in his time. In 1821 he was appointed physician to [[George IV]]. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1788 after a study of the cuckoo, which showed that the newly hatched cuckoo pushes its host's eggs and chicks out of the nest. In 2002 he was named in the [[BBC]]'s list of the 100 Greatest Britons.

American broadcast journalist and war correspondent. Born Egbert Roscoe Murrow in North Carolina to [[Quakers|Quaker]] parents, he gained prominence during [[World War II]] with live radio broadcasts from London amid the [[The Blitz|Blitz]] for [[CBS]], where he worked for his entire career. He recruited a team of war correspondents known as the Murrow Boys. A pioneer of radio and television news, he produced reports on his program *See It Now* that helped lead to the censure of Senator [[Joseph McCarthy]]. The film *Good Night, and Good Luck* takes its name from his signature sign-off phrase. Fellow journalists considered him one of journalism's greatest figures.

Palestinian-American academic and literary critic. As a professor of literature at [[Columbia University]], where he taught from 1963 to 2003, he was among the founders of postcolonial studies. His book *Orientalism* (1978) critiqued how the [[Western world|Western world]] perceived the Orient, and it transformed academic work in literary theory and [[Middle East|Middle Eastern]] studies. Born in [[Jerusalem]], he was a United States citizen through his father, who had served in the U.S. Army in World War I. He graduated from [[Princeton University]] in 1957 and received his doctorate from [[Harvard University]] in 1964. As a political activist he supported a two-state solution and resigned from the Palestinian National Council in 1993 over his criticism of the [[Oslo Accords]]. Some critics have questioned the book's selective use of evidence.

American former intelligence contractor. In 2013 he gave journalists thousands of classified documents from the [[National Security Agency|NSA]], revealing global surveillance programs, many run by the NSA and the Five Eyes alliance with the cooperation of telecommunications companies. Charged under the Espionage Act, he stayed for about a month in Moscow's Sheremetyevo airport before being granted asylum. He became a naturalized Russian citizen in 2022.

Hungarian-American theoretical physicist and chemical engineer. Known as "the father of the hydrogen bomb," he helped devise the Teller–Ulam design with Stanisław Ulam. He was an early member of the [[Manhattan Project]], which developed the atomic bomb, and he supported the George shot of Operation Greenhouse, which produced the world's first thermonuclear burn. He co-founded the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. His extension of [[Enrico Fermi]]'s theory of beta decay was an important step in its application, and in 1953 he co-authored a paper that started the use of the [[Monte Carlo method]] in statistical mechanics. He advocated nuclear power and a strong nuclear arsenal, and he supported [[Ronald Reagan]]'s Strategic Defense Initiative. His testimony at the 1954 security clearance hearing of [[J. Robert Oppenheimer]] expressed doubts about Oppenheimer's trustworthiness, and the clearance was revoked. His advocacy of controversial proposals, including Project Chariot, a plan to excavate an artificial harbor in [[Alaska]] with a thermonuclear explosive, drew criticism.

American psychologist who spent nearly his entire career at [[Columbia University|Teachers College, Columbia University]]. His work on animal learning led to his "theory of connectionism" and his law of effect, which holds that satisfying outcomes strengthen stimulus–response connections. His doctoral dissertation, *Animal Intelligence*, was the first in psychology to use nonhuman subjects, and he used puzzle boxes to test whether animals learned by imitation or observation. He is considered a pioneer of [[Behaviorism]] and helped lay the foundation of educational psychology. He also developed standardized tests for reading and arithmetic. He served as president of the American Psychological Association in 1912. A 2002 survey ranked him the ninth-most cited psychologist of the 20th century.

King of the United Kingdom (r. 1936). He abdicated in December 1936 after his proposal to marry the American divorcee Wallis Simpson was opposed by the prime ministers of the United Kingdom and the Dominions, and it conflicted with his role as titular head of the [[Church of England]]. He was succeeded by his younger brother, [[George VI]]. With a reign of 326 days, he was one of the shortest-reigning British monarchs. As Duke of Windsor he married Simpson in France in 1937, and the couple's visit to Nazi Germany that year fed rumors that he was a Nazi sympathizer.

King of the United Kingdom (r. 1901–1910). Eldest son of [[Queen Victoria]] and [[Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha|Prince Albert]], he was Prince of Wales for almost 60 years and was largely excluded from political influence during his mother's reign. As king he was an effective constitutional monarch who strengthened the popularity of the monarchy and fostered good relations with France, earning the nickname "Peacemaker." He re-instituted traditional ceremonies as public displays. The Edwardian era, which covered his reign, is named after him.

King of England and Ireland (r. 1547–1553). The only surviving son of [[Henry VIII]], he was the first English monarch raised as a Protestant. A regency council governed for him, led first by his uncle Edward Seymour, Duke of Somerset, and then by John Dudley, Duke of Northumberland. Protestantism was established during his reign, with the abolition of clerical celibacy and the Latin Mass. In 1553 he named Lady Jane Grey his heir, excluding his half-sisters, [[Mary I]] and Elizabeth. Mary reversed his Protestant reforms during her reign.

English prince and military commander, heir apparent of [[Edward III]]. One of the most successful English commanders of the [[Hundred Years' War]], he was regarded by English contemporaries as a model of [[Chivalry|chivalry]], while French sources remember him for his brutality. He commanded the vanguard at Crécy and captured King John II of France at Poitiers. He was made Prince of Aquitaine and Gascony in 1362. He died before his father, so his son Richard II succeeded Edward III instead.

King of the English (r. 1042–1066). The last reigning monarch of the [[Wessex|House of Wessex]], he restored its rule after the period of Danish rule that began with [[Cnut]]'s conquest in 1016. He rebuilt [[Westminster Abbey]] as a Romanesque church. Historians disagree about his reign: some see it as leading to the decline of royal power, while others portray him as a successful and sometimes ruthless king. Pope Alexander III canonized him in 1161, and his feast day is 13 October. The [[Norman Conquest]] followed his death, when [[William the Conqueror]] defeated Harold Godwinson at [[Battle of Hastings|Hastings]].

American astronomer who played a crucial role in establishing extragalactic astronomy and observational cosmology. He proved that many objects classified as nebulae were galaxies beyond the [[Milky Way]]. He used the relationship between a [[Cepheid variable|Cepheid variable's]] luminosity and pulsation period to scale galactic and extragalactic distances. In 1929 he confirmed that a galaxy's recessional velocity increases with its distance from Earth, a finding known as [[Hubble's law]], which [[Georges Lemaître]] had proposed two years earlier. The law implies that the universe is expanding. He also devised a classification of galaxies as elliptical, spiral or barred. The [[Hubble Space Telescope]] was named in his honor.

Ray-finned fish of the order *Anguilliformes*, which comprises eight suborders, 20 families, 164 genera and about 1,000 species. Eels are elongated, with no pelvic fins and often no pectoral fins, and their dorsal and anal fins are fused with the tail. Most are marine, though the catadromous genus *Anguilla* lives mostly in freshwater and returns to the sea to breed. Eels begin life as transparent larvae called *leptocephali*, which drift in surface waters before metamorphosing into elvers that climb upstream. Most species are nocturnal predators. The term is also used for other eel-shaped fish, such as [[Electric eel|electric eels]]. The earliest fossil eels are known from the [[Cretaceous]] of Lebanon.

Female reproductive cell, or gamete, of most anisogamous organisms, which reproduce sexually with a larger female gamete and a smaller male one. The egg cell is produced and develops in the [[Ovary|ovary]], and when it fuses with a [[Sperm]] during fertilization, the resulting diploid zygote grows into a new organism. Animal egg cells are also called *ova*, from the Latin word for "egg." In mammals the ovum is fertilized inside the female body, while bird eggs contain enough yolk to nourish the chick through incubation. The doctrine *ex ovo omne vivum* ("every living animal comes from an egg"), associated with [[William Harvey]], rejected spontaneous generation. The human ovum measures about 120 μm in diameter.
